cards.title: Set up a Clarity review around ecommerce friction signals
cards.summary: Use a long enough Clarity sample window for context, but prioritize behavioural Insights and the recordings behind them to find purchase-path friction.
cards.use_when: Beginning a Microsoft Clarity review of a store's homepage, collection pages, PDPs, cart, or checkout and deciding what to inspect first.
steps: Open the Clarity dashboard and set the longest representative date range available. The source commonly uses roughly six months; if installation is newer, use the available period, such as 90 days.

Use dashboard metrics such as sessions, active time, pages per session, device, channel, campaign, browser, and popular pages as context. These overlap with analytics platforms and are not Clarity's distinctive value.

Prioritize Clarity's Insights: rage clicks, dead clicks, excessive scrolling, and quick backs. These identify behaviours that can indicate a shopper is blocked, confused, or searching for purchase-critical information.
Open the recordings attached to an insight before proposing a change. A percentage alone cannot reveal whether the interaction is a genuine conversion barrier or intentional behaviour.

Start on the store's highest-value and highest-traffic journeys: homepage or campaign landing page, collection page, PDP, cart, and checkout. Record the page, device, and apparent blocker for each recurring pattern.
caveats: The six-month period is the presenter's working habit, not a required sample size; major merchandising, site, or traffic changes can make an older window less representative.
Do not discard top-line metrics entirely. They provide useful segmentation and context for behavioural findings.

cards.title: Investigate rage clicks as blocked purchase actions or failed exits
cards.summary: Repeated clicks often indicate a shopper cannot dismiss an interruption or complete an expected action, so use recordings to locate and remove the obstruction.
cards.use_when: Triaging Clarity rage-click Insights on PDPs, cart, checkout, collection filters, promotional popups, or chat widgets.
steps: Treat a rage click as repeated clicking on an element, commonly because the shopper is trying to dismiss an experience or force an expected action.
Open the linked recordings and identify the clicked element, the page context, and what the shopper attempted immediately before and after the clicks.

Check frequent ecommerce causes: a popup appearing in the first three to five seconds before shoppers can assess the page, a chat widget covering add-to-cart or checkout controls, or a dismiss/close control that is difficult to use on mobile.
Prioritize a fix where the interaction obstructs an essential path: viewing product details, selecting a variant, adding to cart, editing the cart, or submitting checkout.
Use the source's rough heuristic only as context: under about 1–2% rage clicks was considered good, but fix a fundamental usability defect even if its measured rate is low.
After changing the experience, review fresh recordings to verify that shoppers can exit or proceed without repeated clicking.
caveats: The 1–2% figure is a presenter heuristic, not a universal benchmark.
Repeated clicks can have different causes; do not assume every rage click is caused by a popup without watching the associated sessions.

cards.title: Classify dead clicks by whether the shopper expected a useful action
cards.summary: A dead click matters when a non-interactive element appears to offer product, navigation, or checkout help that shoppers reasonably expect to access.
cards.use_when: Reviewing dead-click Insights or click maps to decide whether a store element should become clickable, be redesigned, or remain intentionally static.
steps: Define a dead click as a click on an element that has no action. Common store examples include trust badges, featured-in logos, product imagery, informational checkmarks, pricing copy, or a logo that does not return users to the homepage.

Inspect the click map and linked recordings to determine what shoppers expected. A click on an image may signal a desire for a gallery or zoom; a click on delivery copy may signal a desire for shipping details; a checkout logo click may signal a desire to return to browsing.

Keep some elements intentionally non-clickable when linking away would take shoppers out of the purchase path, such as external press logos. Make their non-interactive nature visually clear if they repeatedly attract clicks.
Treat an expected but missing action as a conversion hypothesis. Add an appropriate destination, disclosure, interaction, or clearer affordance, then validate with new recordings.
Do not rely on a dead-click percentage alone; judge the severity by whether the missing action blocks product evaluation or progress toward purchase.
caveats: The source provides no acceptable dead-click-rate threshold.
Not every clicked element should become a link; adding unnecessary links can distract shoppers or fragment the purchase journey.

cards.title: Use excessive scrolling and quick backs to find missing PDP information
cards.summary: Rapid searching or immediate backtracking often means a shopper could not find expected details such as price, reviews, delivery information, variants, or the add-to-cart control.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why shoppers leave PDPs, return to collection pages, or skim product information without progressing to cart.
steps: Treat excessive scrolling as search behaviour: shoppers may be hunting for reviews, price, delivery details, sizing, variants, the add-to-cart control, or an answer buried in a long content block.
Treat a quick back as a visit that rapidly returns to the previous page. On a PDP, this can mean the shopper expected key product information and did not find it immediately.
Open the matching recordings to distinguish between a genuine information gap and normal comparison shopping across products.
Cross-check the scroll map. A sharp drop immediately after a dense paragraph or expandable content area suggests that format or placement is suppressing reach.
Cross-check the click map for attention concentrated on non-clickable product details, review summaries, images, or delivery claims.

Form a specific hypothesis rather than redesigning around the metric: for example, move review proof or price higher, make sizing easier to find, shorten a long paragraph, or make the product gallery interactive. Recheck recordings after release.
caveats: The source gives no numerical threshold for quick backs and does not establish that every quick back is a defect.
A very small excessive-scrolling rate may not be a priority, but a confirmed usability problem should still be corrected.

cards.title: Read click, scroll, and Area Maps against the page's core shopping action
cards.summary: Define the one action a page should advance, then use maps to see whether shoppers reach it, click it, or are diverted by misleading and redundant elements.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing a CRO hypothesis for a homepage, campaign landing page, collection page, PDP, cart, or checkout.
steps: Before opening the map, name the page's core shopping action: browse a collection, select a product, add to cart, begin checkout, or complete a purchase.

On the click map, check whether shoppers click the intended action and whether they click visual elements that are not interactive. The source prefers roughly 5–7% click-through on a core CTA, but also described about 4–5% as average to good; use these only as directional heuristics.
On the scroll map, inspect the top plus the 75%, 50%, and 25% reach checkpoints. Identify whether shoppers can actually reach the proof, product detail, add-to-cart area, or next step.
Use Area Maps when a decision concerns particular regions. Create areas for navigation, delivery filters, sticky controls, banners, or product-card elements and compare their click share.

Flag high-click static elements that look like controls, and low-use redundant elements that add visual weight without helping shoppers proceed. Confirm the pattern in recordings before removing, relocating, or making an element interactive.
caveats: Click-share figures from the source are examples from individual sites, not storewide targets.
Heatmaps identify behavioural patterns, not causality. Pair them with recordings and, where appropriate, a controlled test.

cards.title: Move purchase-critical value and proof into the first viewport when maps show it is unseen
cards.summary: If scroll data shows shoppers rarely reach trust, value, or product-decision content, test moving the highest-value material closer to the top rather than assuming visitors will scroll.
cards.use_when: Auditing homepage, product landing page, collection, or PDP hierarchy and deciding what must appear before the shopper scrolls.
steps: Use your own scroll map to measure how many shoppers reach reviews, ratings, delivery promises, guarantees, product benefits, comparison information, or add-to-cart controls.
The source's rule of thumb is that about 60% of visitors may not scroll past the top section. Treat this as a prompt to inspect your store data, not as a universal statistic.
If important proof is only reached by a small minority, test moving it earlier in the experience. The source's example interpreted roughly 30% testimonial reach as a placement problem.
Make the first viewport quickly answer the ecommerce equivalents of: what is this product or category, who is it for, why should I care, and why should I trust this store?

Use concrete trust and risk-reduction material where substantiated: review count and rating, relevant buyer proof, a guarantee or trial, shipping information, and clear return terms. The source highlighted these patterns in brand examples, not as required minimums.
Recheck scroll reach, CTA engagement, and recordings after the new hierarchy is live.
caveats: The source's 60% no-scroll figure is presented as a general statistic and should be verified against the store's own data.
Do not overload the hero with every proof element; the source supports moving high-value content up, not adding indiscriminate clutter.

cards.title: Diagnose sharp scroll drop-offs after long product copy
cards.summary: When scroll reach collapses immediately after a long block of text, simplify or restructure the content so shoppers can reach the next purchase decision.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a PDP or product landing page where the add-to-cart area, reviews, specifications, or related products receive unexpectedly little reach.
steps: Read the scroll map as a sequence of checkpoints rather than a single average. Locate the exact section after which reach falls sharply.
Compare the drop with the page content. In the source's PDP example, reach was high before a long paragraph and then fell substantially, leaving only about 25% of visitors reaching add to cart.

Treat a sudden post-copy drop as a hypothesis that the text is intimidating, overly dense, or delaying information shoppers need. Cut nonessential wording, turn key points into scannable blocks, or relocate detail behind an intentional disclosure if appropriate.

Check recordings to see whether shoppers skim past, pause, repeatedly scroll, or leave at that section. This helps distinguish copy overload from another issue such as an unavailable option or an unexpected price.
Compare the shape of the drop with other sections and pages so you do not mistake normal page-end decay for a content problem.
After release, measure whether more shoppers reach the next decision point and whether the revised section still answers the questions shoppers seek.
caveats: The source's high-reach-to-25% example is one client observation, not a benchmark.
Long copy is not inherently harmful; detailed products may require it, but the presentation must support scanning and progression.

cards.title: Run focused recording reviews until the purchase-path pattern is clear
cards.summary: Watch recordings with a deliberate why mindset and stop when recurring purchase friction is understood, then repeat after changes rather than chasing an arbitrary viewing count.
cards.use_when: Planning a qualitative review of recordings from shoppers who browse products, add to cart, abandon cart, or struggle in checkout.
steps: Reserve a focused review block; the source uses one to two hours without distractions. Begin with the store pages most consequential to purchase: homepage or campaign landing page, collection, PDP, cart, and checkout.

Watch each session by asking why: why did the shopper click this, skip that section, return to a prior page, repeatedly scroll, or leave at this moment? Capture the inferred reason only when the behaviour supports it.
Look for recurring friction: dead clicks, rage clicks, navigation loops, rapid search scrolling, product-option confusion, filters that disappear during browsing, and cart or checkout interruptions.
Track the actual path into each key page. For example, identify whether shoppers reach a PDP from navigation, a product card, search, a promotional CTA, or an external landing page.
Do not set a fixed recording quota. The source has watched roughly 100 sessions in some cases and 400–450 in others; stop when additional sessions become repetitive and the main pattern is clear.
After a change ships, begin a new review of fresh sessions to check whether the behaviour changed and to surface the next constraint.
caveats: Recording review is qualitative evidence, not proof that a proposed change will increase conversion or revenue.
Long sessions can reflect high intent, confusion, comparison behaviour, or inactivity; interpret duration in context.

cards.title: Compare engaged and disengaged sessions with Clarity sorts and filters
cards.summary: Review both high-activity and low-activity shopper sessions to understand successful browsing paths as well as sessions that fail to progress.
cards.use_when: Building a purposeful recording sample instead of watching sessions at random, especially for collection-to-PDP-to-cart journeys.
steps: In the recordings view, sort by clicks high-to-low and pages high-to-low to inspect highly active browsing sessions. These can reveal how shoppers successfully discover products, use filters, and move through the store.

Reverse the sorts—clicks low-to-high and pages low-to-high—to inspect low-engagement sessions. Look for immediate exits, lack of product discovery, blocked interactions, or confusion at a key entry page.
Compare the two groups on the same page type. Ask what controls, information, or page paths are available to progressing shoppers that are missed or unclear for disengaged shoppers.

Use filters such as device, landing page, scroll depth, page duration, performance or speed, and user actions to make each recording answer a defined question, such as whether mobile shoppers can use collection filters or whether a campaign landing page leads to PDP views.
Use skip-inactivity only when rapidly reviewing a long session. Leave inactivity visible when it may reveal hesitation, reading, interrupted checkout, or an unresponsive interface.
Verify current Clarity labels and filter options in the interface before documenting a repeatable workflow.
caveats: Sorting by clicks or pages can reflect page complexity rather than intent, so compare behaviour in page context.
The source's interface labels may change over time.

cards.title: Fix collection controls that shoppers repeatedly scroll back to reach
cards.summary: Repeated travel from a product list back to the top for the same control indicates that the control is not available where shoppers need it.
cards.use_when: Reviewing collection or catalog recordings in which shoppers browse products, scroll back to filters or sorting, and then resume browsing.
steps: Watch collection-page recordings for a repeated pattern: the shopper scrolls through products, returns to the top, changes a filter, delivery option, sort, or category control, then scrolls down again.

Confirm what the shopper is returning for. In the source's on-demand delivery example, a menu filter existed only at the top, making it unavailable while the visitor evaluated items lower on the page.
Frame the issue as control visibility and access, not necessarily weak copy. The shopper already demonstrates interest in using the control.

Check whether the pattern occurs across several sessions, device types, and collection depths before prioritizing it. Mobile behaviour may be especially important if the control consumes substantial top-of-page space.
Test an appropriate persistent or easier-to-reopen control, such as a sticky filter or sort trigger, while preserving product-list space and avoiding obstruction of add-to-cart controls.
After release, inspect fresh recordings to see whether shoppers can refine the assortment without repeated scroll-back and whether they continue toward PDPs and cart.
caveats: A sticky filter is the source's proposed remedy, not a tested universal solution.
Do not infer a usability issue from one return-to-top action; shoppers may also be intentionally restarting their browse.

cards.title: Turn Clarity evidence into a testable ecommerce hypothesis
cards.summary: Move from maps and recordings to a single observable change hypothesis tied to shopper reach, interaction, and purchase-path progression.
cards.use_when: Converting Clarity findings into a prioritized experiment or implementation brief for a PDP, collection, cart, checkout, or landing page.
steps: Define the page's single intended progression: view a product, select a variant, add to cart, begin checkout, or complete checkout.

Use click and scroll maps to establish whether shoppers reach the relevant section and interact with the intended element. Locate the most specific apparent barrier, such as a long block before add to cart, a hidden filter, a misleading static banner, or missing delivery information.
Open recordings for the same page, device, and behaviour to validate that the map pattern reflects actual shopper friction and to understand the likely intent.

Write a focused hypothesis in change-and-reason form: for example, 'Because shoppers repeatedly return to the top to change the collection filter, test a persistent filter trigger so refinements remain available while browsing products.'

Specify the behaviour to evaluate after release: reach to add-to-cart, CTA click share, filter use without scroll-back, PDP views from collection, cart starts, checkout progression, or purchase conversion. Choose the metric appropriate to the page's role.
Use this qualitative evidence to prioritize the test, then apply the store's normal experiment design and sample-size calculation before making causal claims about conversion or revenue.
caveats: Clarity demonstrates behaviour and supports hypotheses; it does not by itself establish causality or statistical significance.
The source demonstrates the diagnostic loop but does not provide experiment outcomes or a statistical testing design.

Choose the metric appropriate to the page's role.","Use this qualitative evidence to prioritize the test, then apply the store's normal experiment design and sample-size calculation before making causal claims about conversion or revenue."],"caveats":["Clarity demonstrates behaviour and supports hypotheses; it does not by itself establish causality or statistical significance.","The source demonstrates the diagnostic loop but does not provide experiment outcomes or a statistical testing design."],"tags":["testing","microsoft-clarity","experiment-design","conversion-optimization","heatmaps","session-recordings","measurement"]}]}

input.source_name: Microsoft Clarity COMPLETE Tutorial in 2026 to Skyrocket Conversions.docx

cards.title: Set up Clarity analysis with a 6-month sample window
cards.summary: Start any Clarity review by setting a sample period of roughly the last 6 months, or 90 days if setup limits you, and focus on the Insights block rather than baseline KPIs.
cards.use_when: Beginning a session-recording/heatmap review of a site in Microsoft Clarity and deciding which date range and dashboard panel to work from.
steps: Open the main Clarity dashboard and set the date range to roughly the last 6 months of data; the source uses that as a general sample (it does not have to be exact).
If Clarity was only recently installed, fall back to the longest available window such as last 90 days.

Treat the top-line metrics — scroll depth, active time, pages per session, total sessions, smart events, referrer/channel, campaign, browser, device and popular-pages data — as baseline KPIs you can already get from Google Analytics.
Concentrate attention on the Insights block: rage clicks, dead clicks, excessive scrolling, quick backs, since those are what makes Clarity distinctive.
Watch the matching recordings behind any insight that warrants a change rather than acting on the percentage alone.
caveats: The 6-month window is the presenter's habit and may not be possible depending on when tracking was installed.
The dashboard overlap metrics remain useful as context — their inclusion does not mean they are unusable.

cards.title: Interpret rage clicks as failed exits
cards.summary: Rage clicks are repeated clicks on an element, usually to escape a popup, chat widget or blocked action; they are a friction signal worth watching even when the rate looks low.
cards.use_when: Triaging the Clarity Insights block or filtering recordings for frustration before forming a test hypothesis.
steps: Read rage clicks as people clicking an element multiple times, typically trying to exit an experience.
Check common triggers: a popup that lands in the first 3-5 seconds before the visitor has scrolled, or a chat bot/interstitial blocking an add-to-cart or form submit (especially on B2B sites).
Click the camera icon beside the rage-click insight to open the recordings page and watch the sessions that produced them.
Judge the rate against the presenter's heuristic: under roughly 1-2% is generally considered good; the source's example was 0.2%.
Resolve fundamental usability issues regardless of percentage — a low rate does not excuse a broken exit path.
caveats: The 1-2% good rate is a presenter heuristic, not a benchmark with evidence.
Low rates do not mean there is nothing to fix; the source explicitly says metrics matter less than fundamental usability.

cards.title: Classify dead clicks and decide which to keep
cards.summary: Dead clicks are clicks on elements that are not clickable; some are acceptable (logos you deliberately don't link out) while others signal missing functionality that blocks conversion.
cards.use_when: Reviewing dead-click insights or heatmaps and deciding whether an element should become clickable.
steps: Understand a dead click as a click on an element that is not clickable — e.g. 'As Seen On' or 'As Featured In' logos, informational checkmarks, or a non-clickable site logo.
Accept some dead clicks deliberately: if linking out would send people away from the conversion path, keeping 'As Seen On' logos non-clickable can be a reasonable choice.

Treat other dead clicks as defects: if clicking would genuinely help the user proceed (pricing details, product information, returning to the homepage from checkout or a product page), the missing link is a conversion barrier.
Investigate with the click map, then validate with recordings before changing anything — the source saw logo clicks from both checkout and product pages.
caveats: The source gives no threshold for an acceptable dead-click rate; whether to act depends on whether the element would help conversion.
Deciding which elements 'should' be clickable is a judgement call beyond the examples given.

cards.title: Read excessive scrolling as search behaviour
cards.summary: Excessive scrolling means users skim rapidly top-to-bottom, usually because they cannot find reviews, price, a CTA, or because a text block is too long.
cards.use_when: Interpreting Clarity's 'excessive scrolling' insight or watching recordings where users move through a page unusually fast.
steps: Treat excessive scrolling as a symptom that the user is hunting for something they cannot find.
Check the candidate causes the source lists: looking for reviews, looking for the add-to-cart button or the price, or skimming past a long undifferentiated block of text.
Cross-check with the scroll map: if engagement drops sharply after a specific long paragraph, the block itself is likely the cause.
Cross-check with the click map to see whether the missing element (price, CTA, review score) is drawing attention elsewhere.
Act when the underlying issue is real even if the excessive-scrolling percentage is tiny — the source's example sat under 0.01%.
caveats: Different causes require different fixes; do not assume one; the source does not state a rule for distinguishing them.
A sub-0.01% rate was not treated as a priority in the source's example, but usability defects are still resolved.

cards.title: Read quick backs as missing expected information
cards.summary: Quick backs are visits that immediately return to the previous page, usually because the page did not contain the information the user went there to find.
cards.use_when: Reviewing quick-back insights, especially on product pages, or diagnosing back-and-forth navigation in recordings.
steps: Define a quick back as a user going to a page and then rapidly returning to the previous one.
Derive the likely cause: the user expected specific information on that page and could not find it immediately, so they bounce back and forth.
Apply it most often to product pages, where shoppers look for a specific detail and leave if it is absent.
Watch the recordings for quick backs, since Clarity can open the matching sessions from the insight.
If the same page accumulates quick backs, treat the missing information as the hypothesis to test rather than redesigning on the metric alone.
caveats: The source gives no numeric threshold for quick backs and prescribes no specific fix.
Quick backs can also reflect honest comparison shopping between pages, not necessarily a defect.

cards.title: Change the Clarity screenshot before reading heatmaps
cards.summary: Heatmaps sometimes render a popup or broken layout; use the change-screenshot control to pick the design variation you actually want to analyse.
cards.use_when: Opening the heatmap tab in Clarity and finding the screenshot does not match the page you expected.
steps: Open the heatmap tab and pick a page from the popular-pages list (typically the 5-10 highest-traffic pages are listed).
If the screenshot shows a popup, an interstitial, or a misconfigured section, click the change screenshot button in the top right.

Browse the list of design variations on the left and select the version that matches the real page experience — for example the version without the popup, or a version that includes the navigation menu.
Use a navigation-inclusive screenshot when you specifically want to see where clicks go within the menu.
Then choose the device filter — desktop, tablet, mobile — based on which source drives the most traffic for the site.
caveats: The source gives no criteria beyond matching the actual experience or deliberately inspecting navigation clicks.
The source's example account only listed two pages, which it notes is not typical.

cards.title: Use click and scroll maps to test the core action
cards.summary: When reading a click map, first identify the one core action the page wants, then check whether users reach and click it; low CTA click-through signals a hero or layout problem.
cards.use_when: Analysing a homepage, landing page or product page heatmap and deciding what to test first.
steps: Name the single core action the page is for (e.g. sign-up, add to cart, booking) before looking at the data.

Check what share of clicks lands on that CTA. The source's rough benchmark: 5-7% click-through is what they like to see; the Clarity example totalled around 4-5% across the button area, described as average-to-good; they have seen client sites below 1-3%.

Note clicks landing where nothing exists, or on non-interactive elements — e.g. informational checkmarks, headline and body text, or an image that is not a control. Those are candidate features to add (the source hypothesises an explanatory video where an image attracts clicks).
Switch to the scroll map and read the 75%/50%/25% checkpoints plus the top of page to see where people drop off.
State the hypothesis in terms of the goal: if people are not reaching the CTA, what fundamental change would get them there?
caveats: 5-7% is the presenter's preference, not an evidence-based standard; 4-5% was still called good.
Do not redesign from heatmap data alone — the source's own workflow combines maps and recordings, with copy/UI changes handled outside this step.

cards.title: Use the 60% no-scroll rule to prioritise above the fold
cards.summary: Most visitors never scroll past the top section, so value proposition and social proof must be established in the first five seconds and higher-value content moved up.
cards.use_when: Deciding what content belongs above the fold, or justifying moving testimonials, reviews or key information up the page.
steps: Work from the presenter's statistical rule of thumb: about 60% of people never scroll past the very top section, so most of your services, case studies, testimonials or product detail below it will never be seen.
Apply it to your own scroll map: if only about 30% of people reach the testimonials, treat that as a placement problem.
Move important proof higher — the source's conclusion from 30% reach on testimonials was to bring that content up the page experience.

Ensure the hero explains who you are, what you do, and what is in it for me in five seconds or less; the source warns that without it you see a large drop-off immediately after the hero (the healthy alternative being roughly 93-95% continuing).
Give cold users a reason to trust you early: the source's principle is that a cold visitor knows nothing about you, so social proof above the fold is what makes them scroll.
caveats: The 60% figure is presented as a general statistic, not measured from every account; verify against your own scroll map.
The 93-95% continuation figure came from a demo account and is illustrative, not a target.

cards.title: Use social proof examples to design above-the-fold trust
cards.summary: Reviews, ratings, buyer counts and featured-in placements are the proof patterns the source shows working above the fold for DTC and B2B sites.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the hero section's trust signals for ecommerce, SaaS or B2B.
steps: Put review counts and ratings in or near the hero. Source examples: Mudwater with 49,000+ reviews plus a testimonial and featured-in placements; Iris (laser device) with 26,000+ reviews, 4.6 star rating, 'most trusted' positioning and a 365-day trial with free shipping; ZoomInfo with 8,000+ G2 reviews and 35,000+ businesses; Clarity with a 4.8/5 G2 rating.
Pair volume proof with risk reduction where possible — the source highlights Iris's 365-day trial and free shipping as fear-reduction and certainty elements.
For B2B, third-party review platforms such as G2 and buyer counts performed the same role as DTC review counts.
Check whether proof is actually above the fold: use the scroll map to see whether the proof section is reached by a large share, and move it up if not.
Treat all named figures as the source's examples of well-known brands, not benchmarks you must match.
caveats: The external ratings and review counts in the source are not independently verified and will age.
The source does not specify minimum volumes or exact placement beyond above the fold.

cards.title: Use Area Maps to quantify clicks per element
cards.summary: Clarity's Area Map breaks the page into named regions and reports the share of clicks each receives, making redundant and misleading elements visible.
cards.use_when: Deciding which page elements to keep, move or remove, or investigating a UI element that looks interactive.
steps: Open the Area view, then click edit areas and draw the regions you want to compare (e.g. two menu options side by side, a sticky filter, the top navigation, a banner).
Read the click share per area. Source example: 'on demand' (immediate delivery) took 4% of clicks versus 1.74% for a non-immediate full-menu option, which matched expectations but quantified the gap.

Flag any element with a large click share that is not interactive — the source's example was a 'your browsing' banner that looked like a button, absorbed 46% of clicks, and caused users to leave in frustration once they realised it did nothing.
Flag redundant elements with very few clicks and remove them; the source's stated principle is that less is more in UX for conversion.
Note useful benchmarks from the source's example: 8.48% of clicks on the top navigation and 5.58% on a sticky filter in the bottom right.
Confirm any suspected issue with recordings or user testing before changing the design.
caveats: The click-share percentages come from individual unnamed client sites and vary by page and traffic.
The source does not define a threshold for 'very few clicks'; removal is a judgement call.

cards.title: Diagnose sharp scroll drop-offs after long text blocks
cards.summary: Scroll-map checkpoints reveal where readers abandon, and the source's product-page example shows a long paragraph cutting reach from the high 80s/90s down to around 25%.
cards.use_when: Analysing a product page or any content-heavy page where you suspect a wall of text is suppressing reach.
steps: Read the scroll map's checkpoints rather than just the single average fold line, so you can locate the step change.
In the source's product-page example, roughly 93% reached one point, then about a 30% drop followed a long paragraph, and only about 25% reached the add-to-cart area.
Interpret a step drop immediately after a text block as that block intimidating or overwhelming readers; the recommended action is to cut the text down substantially.
Check that the drop is not simply the natural decay of the page by comparing the shape to the content section it falls after.
Do the same analysis on other high-traffic pages: homepage, product, checkout for ecommerce; homepage, contact, get-a-quote, service pages for B2B.
Combine the scroll evidence with recordings before rewriting, so the cut is aimed at what readers were actually looking for.
caveats: The 93%-to-25% figures are from one client example, not a benchmark.
A drop at a checkpoint is not automatically a defect — it can reflect the natural end of useful content.

cards.title: Move forms above redundant 'Contact Us' headings on B2B pages
cards.summary: A generic 'Contact Us' or 'Get Started' headline at the top of a B2B contact page wastes the fold and was associated with roughly 25% immediate drop-off before the form was seen.
cards.use_when: Auditing a B2B contact, get-a-quote or demo page where the form sits below the first screen.
steps: Check the scroll/heat data for the contact page: the source's example showed approximately 25% of visitors dropping off immediately, never reaching the form because a large 'Contact Us' headline occupied the top of the page.

Recognise the pattern as recurring across B2B sites: headlines like contact us, get started, sign up now, partner with us at the very top, which the source calls redundant because the visitor already knows they are on the contact page.
Test a layout where the form is moved up into the space currently spent on the redundant heading.
Use the reclaimed space for a compelling value proposition instead of restating the page purpose.
Validate by re-checking scroll reach of the form field area and by watching recordings of the new version.
caveats: The source does not state the outcome of moving the form up; this is a proposed test, not a proven result.
The 25% drop-off came from one unnamed B2B client example.

cards.title: Simplify forms and reduce phone-number requests
cards.summary: The source's form guidance is four fields or fewer, no phone number unless sales genuinely needs it, and a check of where in the form people abandon.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a lead form, demo-request or wholesale enquiry form that is underperforming.
steps: Audit the number of fields. The source commonly sees 8-10 fields, and observes that most users do not get past the third or fourth.
Cut to four fields or fewer, which the source calls the typical sweet spot.

Remove the phone number field unless it is absolutely necessary to the sales team — the source attributes substantial drop-off specifically to phone-number requests, including for ecommerce businesses with a wholesale enquiry flow.
Find the field where abandonment happens and treat that field as the suspect.
Analyse how people actually reach the form page, not just what happens once they are on it, so the journey to the form is also part of the diagnosis.
caveats: Four fields or fewer is described as 'typically' the sweet spot, not a universal rule; a genuinely qualified B2B lead may need more.
The phone-number finding is based on the source's repeated observation, not on a controlled test.

cards.title: Apply heatmap and area-map use cases for ecommerce and B2B
cards.summary: The source catalogues the specific analysis jobs heatmaps and scroll maps support: content engagement, navigation, CTA placement, form completion, journey flow and visual hierarchy.
cards.use_when: Planning what to extract from Clarity for an ecommerce store, a B2B site, or a hybrid with a wholesale arm.
steps: Content engagement: identify which products, images, case studies, white papers or service descriptions draw the most attention and clicks; if a frequently clicked section sits low, consider bringing it higher.

Navigation: find the most-clicked navigation elements and product or collection pages, then use that to optimise site structure. For SaaS clients the pricing page is frequently the most visited and often the most under-leveraged — tailor it to reduce fear and uncertainty and explain what happens after sign-up.

Action placement: check whether people click the core CTAs at all (add to cart, buy now, sign up, book a demo). If clicks are low, consider more emphasis, a higher position, or different placement and design.
Form completion: trace how users reach the form and where they drop off within it.
User journey and flow: track how people move from homepage to product or service page and through to checkout.
Visual hierarchy: check whether banners, promotional sections and badges are organised clearly top to bottom and actually guide the eye.
caveats: These are candidate use cases, not ranked priorities; the source does not say which to do first.
No specific metric thresholds are offered for each use case.

cards.title: Run a Clarity recording review with a why mindset
cards.summary: Block one to two hours, watch recordings uninterrupted, and interrogate each behaviour with 'why did they do that' rather than cataloguing clicks.
cards.use_when: Sitting down to work through session recordings before forming test hypotheses.
steps: Remove distractions for the next one to two hours and commit to watching recordings only.
Watch with an explicit 'why' mindset: why did this person do this, why did they click here, what could be the possible reasons — this is what turns a recording into an insight.
Start from the crucial pages: for ecommerce, homepage, product and checkout; for B2B, homepage, contact, get-a-quote and service pages.
Watch for friction patterns across recordings: clicks on non-clickable elements, repeated navigation loops, rapid clicking, excessive scrolling and content skimming.
Track navigation flow — did users reach the product via the nav, a CTA button, or by scrolling and then clicking a CTA?
Compare engagement time on sections and look for conversion leaks such as the source's example of a user switching menus, losing their cart despite a warning popup, and leaving after 21 minutes.
Take notes as you go, then combine the recording findings with the heat and scroll maps to build the fuller picture.
caveats: The 1-2 hour focus block is a working habit, not a guarantee of insight.
The cart-loss case study is one client example from an on-demand delivery flow, not a general rule.

cards.title: Decide how many recordings to watch and when to stop
cards.summary: Watch until the main friction pattern is clear — some accounts need about 100 recordings, others 400-450 — then stop, because further viewing becomes repetitive.
cards.use_when: Scoping a session-recording review and deciding when sufficient evidence has been gathered.
steps: Do not fix a target number in advance; the source's practice ranges from about 100 recordings for some clients to 400-450 watched rapidly for others.
Define your stopping rule as the point at which you understand the main patterns — what the main issues and friction points are.
Once that pattern is identified, stop; the source says continued watching gets repetitive at that point.
After shipping site changes, restart the loop and watch recordings of the new version to find further improvements; the source calls this a never-ending game.

Classify behaviour with the available filters (time frame, device, user action, scroll depth, landing page, performance/speed, page duration) so each session you watch answers a question rather than being watched blind.
caveats: 100 and 400-450 are examples, not thresholds, and sample needs vary by traffic and question.
The source does not define a quantitative criterion for 'the main pattern'.

cards.title: Triangulate engaged vs unengaged users with recording sorts
cards.summary: Sort recordings by clicks and pages high-to-low and then low-to-high to compare the most active visitors with the least active ones and see both sides of the behaviour.
cards.use_when: Building a recording sample that reveals both successful and failing sessions rather than only extremes of one kind.
steps: In the recordings screen, open sort and choose clicks high-to-low, then pages high-to-low, to see your most active sessions.
Then reverse both: clicks low-to-high and pages low-to-high, to see the least active sessions.
Compare the two groups to understand what engaged behaviour looks like versus disengaged behaviour on the same pages.
Use the skip-inactivity option when speed-reading a very long session for quick insight; leave it off when you are new to Clarity or need to see the periods where users are not moving at all.
Note that a long session duration is itself a signal of high intent — the source's example was a one-hour mobile session.
Filter by speed when reviewing extremely long recordings so playback is manageable.
caveats: Exact filter names such as the skip-inactivity label and the speed option may differ in the current Clarity interface — verify in the product.
Sorting by clicks favours page complexity as well as intent, so interpret alongside the page in question.

cards.title: Spot non-sticky filters from repeated scroll-back in recordings
cards.summary: When recording after recording shows users scrolling to the bottom and back to the top to reach a filter, the filter's placement is the usability problem, not the copy.
cards.use_when: Reviewing ecommerce or catalogue recordings where users bounce up and down a listing page.
steps: Watch a recording and note repeated cycles of scrolling down through products and back to the top of the page.
Check what the user is returning for — in the source's on-demand delivery example it was a menu filter (on demand versus full menu) that existed only at the top of the page.
Diagnose the cause as a visibility issue: the control the user needs is not reachable from where they are browsing.
Consider making the filter sticky so it remains available while scrolling; the source frames this as a plausible improvement rather than a mandatory fix.
Confirm the pattern across several recordings before treating a single scroll-back as evidence, then validate the change with new recordings after shipping.
caveats: Making the filter sticky is one proposed remedy; the source does not test or confirm its effect.
The example came from an on-demand delivery client, so copy the reasoning rather than the specific fix.

cards.title: Sequence from behavioural data to a testable hypothesis
cards.summary: This workflow turns Clarity evidence into a specific layout hypothesis: identify the goal, find where reach and clicks fall, watch the matching recordings, then state the change to test.
cards.use_when: Converting heatmap, scroll and recording findings into a concrete CRO test rather than a vibe-based redesign.
steps: Set the sample window and identify the page's single core action or goal.
Check whether people reach that section and click that element using the click map and the 75%/50%/25% scroll checkpoints.
Locate the specific blocker: a redundant heading occupying the top of a B2B contact page, a long text block before the add-to-cart, a misplaced CTA, or a filter only available at the top.
Watch the recordings behind the relevant insight to confirm the behaviour and understand the user's intent, using a why mindset.

Write the hypothesis as a change with a reason, e.g. the source's example: a 'Contact Us' header takes too much fold real estate, about 25% of B2B visitors drop off before seeing the form, so test a layout with the form moved up.
State the expected effect on reach or click share so the test can be judged, then combine heatmap, scroll and recording evidence before shipping.
caveats: The source demonstrates the diagnostic loop but does not report test outcomes or statistical designs for these examples.
Copy and UI changes belong to a different stage than the behavioural diagnosis shown here, so hand off once the hypothesis is set.
